To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
T-lymphocytes are altered even in healthy newborns born to HIV-infected mothers and that these abnormalities persist in older HIV-uninfected children.

HIV infection during pregnancy is associated with abnormal immune development in the uninfected newborn, that these abnormalities persist over a period of several years, and that the biologic significance of the abnormalities should be investigated.
HIV infection in the mother may have a direct effect on the immune system of the child.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the immune response to HIV-1 and the immune system in HIV-1 infected individuals, in particular in HIV-1 seropositive women and their uninfected newborn children.

the study of the immunological and virological aspects of the vertical transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and in particular, of the mechanisms that allow the virus to cross the placental barriers and infect the fetus.
the effects of HIV on uninfected children exposed to the virus in utero.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV and its soluble products are capable of inducing immunologic abnormalities in the offspring of infected mothers even in the absence of HIV infection.
the immunological abnormalities found in HIV-uninfacted children born to HIV-infected mothers are not the consequence of the transplacental passage of HIV or of its products.
the T cell immune system is impaired in HIV-exposed but uninfected children and that these abnormalities persist over the first few years of life.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown for the first time that T-cell maturation is impaired in uninfected infants born to HIV-infected mothers.
the immune system of the uninfected newborn of an HIV-infected mother is not fully developed and is altered in a way that may predispose the child to infections and/or other immune-related diseases.

we found that the T-cell maturation abnormalities in HIV-uninfated children of HIV infected mothers were similar to those in HIV infected children and that the abnormalities were partially retained over time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV-infected women can pass on some of the immunological abnormalities to their uninfected offspring.
there is a biological effect of HIV exposure in the womb.
the children who have been exposed to HIV in utero and who are not infected, have a different pattern of lymphocyte development and maturation compared with unexposed children.
